promptUsed: Here's the full source of a GitHub repository — write a guide to help a new contributor understand what it does, set it up, run it, understand its structure, and run its tests.

guide.markdown:
Contributor Guide: Ky

This repository is Ky, a small TypeScript HTTP client built on top of the standard Fetch API. Its goal is to make Fetch more convenient while retaining Fetch's standards-based Request/Response model. The package describes itself as a “tiny and elegant HTTP client based on the Fetch API” and targets modern browsers, Node.js, Bun, and Deno.

The repository is currently version 2.0.2, uses native ES modules, and requires Node.js 22 or newer.

1. What the project does

At a high level, Ky wraps fetch() and adds a higher-level request pipeline:

User calls ky(...)
       │
       ▼
Normalize options
       │
       ├── baseUrl / prefix
       ├── headers / JSON / searchParams
       ├── timeout configuration
       └── hooks
       │
       ▼
beforeRequest hooks
       │
       ▼
fetch()
       │
       ├── network/timeout error ──► retry logic
       │
       └── Response
                │
                ▼
        afterResponse hooks
                │
                ▼
        HTTP error handling
                │
                ▼
          retry if needed
                │
                ▼
        decorated Response
                │
                ▼
       .json() / .text() / etc.

The central implementation is source/core/Ky.ts. Its Ky.create() method constructs the request pipeline, runs initialization and request hooks, performs Fetch, processes responses, handles HTTP errors, invokes retry logic, and decorates the resulting Response with convenience methods.

The important features

A contributor should understand these concepts before modifying the core:

HTTP method shortcuts such as ky.get(), ky.post(), ky.put(), etc.
JSON request/response shortcuts, including .json().
Search parameter handling.
baseUrl and prefix URL resolution.
Retries, including exponential backoff and server-provided retry timing.
Per-attempt and total-operation timeouts.
Request lifecycle hooks.
HTTP/network/timeout-specific errors.
Upload/download progress where the environment supports the necessary streams.
Custom Fetch implementations.
Standard Schema validation for parsed JSON.
Browser compatibility, including browser-specific behavior tested through Playwright.

For example, the API's json option serializes the value and sets the appropriate content type, while searchParams merges URL query parameters.

2. Getting the repository running

Prerequisites

Use:

Node.js 22+
npm
A browser environment capable of running the Playwright browsers if you want the complete test suite.

The package explicitly declares "node": ">=22".
The CI currently tests Node 22, Node 24, and the latest Node release on macOS.

Install dependencies

From the repository root:

npm install

The project intentionally does not maintain a package-lock.json; .npmrc disables package-lock generation, and the lockfile is also ignored by Git.

Because npm install invokes the package's prepare script, it also builds the distribution:

"prepare": "npm run build"

The build itself is:

npm run build

which deletes distribution/ and runs TypeScript using tsconfig.dist.json.

Install Playwright browsers

For the full test environment, run:

npx playwright install --with-deps

This is explicitly done by CI before the test command.

3. Running the project

Ky is a library, not a standalone server or CLI application. There isn't a start command.

The two important contributor commands are:

npm run build
npm test

Build

npm run build

The build takes everything under source/ and emits it into distribution/, with source maps and inline sources enabled.

Conceptually:

source/
   ↓ TypeScript compiler
distribution/
   ├── index.js
   ├── *.js
   ├── *.d.ts
   └── source maps

The published package exposes distribution/index.js and its corresponding TypeScript declarations.

Run the full test suite

npm test

This is important: npm test is not merely "run the tests." It performs three stages:

xo
 ↓
TypeScript build
 ↓
AVA tests

The script is:

"test": "xo && npm run build && ava"

So a successful test run means linting, compilation, and the AVA test suite all passed.

5. Where to look when changing behavior

source/core/Ky.ts — the heart of Ky

If you need to understand how a request actually executes, start here.

Ky is responsible for:

validating and normalizing options;
constructing the native Request;
applying URL options;
setting up abort/timeout handling;
running beforeRequest;
invoking Fetch;
handling retries;
running afterResponse;
turning failed HTTP responses into HTTPError;
decorating responses;
handling response-body shortcuts.

For example, the main request flow calls beforeRequest, then Fetch/retry, then afterResponse, and finally applies HTTP-error behavior.

This is the file to read first for a behavioral bug.

source/core/constants.ts — capability detection and shared constants

This file detects environment capabilities such as:

request streams;
AbortController;
AbortSignal.any;
response streams;
FormData.

It also defines supported HTTP methods and response shortcut types.

The runtime feature detection matters because Ky is intended to operate across browsers and server-side Fetch implementations rather than assuming every Fetch feature exists.

source/core/retry-timing.ts — HTTP retry timing

This isolates interpretation of retry-related HTTP headers.

Ky recognizes Retry-After first, then falls back to rate-limit headers such as RateLimit-Reset, X-RateLimit-Retry-After, and related variants.

The retry system also supports exponential backoff. The documented default delay is:

0.3 × 2^(attempt - 1) × 1000 ms

with configurable limits and jitter.

6. Errors are a separate subsystem

The source/errors/ directory contains the error model:

errors/
├── ForceRetryError.ts
├── HTTPError.ts
├── KyError.ts
├── NetworkError.ts
├── NonError.ts
├── SchemaValidationError.ts
└── TimeoutError.ts

The public API also provides type guards such as:

isKyError()
isHTTPError()
isNetworkError()
isTimeoutError()
isForceRetryError()

These allow callers to distinguish Ky-specific failures from arbitrary exceptions.

A particularly important distinction is:

HTTPError
   └── server responded, but with an unsuccessful status
NetworkError
   └── Fetch failed at the network level
TimeoutError
   └── Ky's timeout machinery aborted the operation
ForceRetryError
   └── internal mechanism for explicitly requesting another attempt

That distinction is important when changing retry behavior because Ky intentionally does not retry arbitrary programming errors.

7. Options and types

Most of the public API's TypeScript contracts live under:

source/types/

Pay particular attention to:

options.ts — Ky options and request configuration.
hooks.ts — hook types.
retry.ts — retry configuration.
ResponsePromise.ts — the special promise returned by Ky.
request.ts / response.ts — request/response-related types.
standard-schema.ts — JSON schema-validation interface.

This is where you should look if you're changing the public API or TypeScript types, rather than merely changing internal implementation.

For example, timeout represents a timeout for an individual attempt, while totalTimeout covers the complete operation, including retries and retry delays.

8. Utilities

source/utils/ contains implementation details that keep Ky.ts manageable:

body.ts              stream/request/response body handling
delay.ts             retry delays
is-network-error.ts  network error identification
is.ts                small type predicates
merge.ts             option/header/hook merging
normalize.ts         option normalization
options.ts           option inspection
timeout.ts           timeout implementation
type-guards.ts       public/internal error checks
types.ts             shared TypeScript helpers

One especially important utility is merge.ts.

Ky's extend() behavior does more than a simple shallow object spread: hooks, headers, search parameters, and other nested options can be merged, with replaceOption() available when replacement rather than merging is desired.

9. source/index.ts — public API boundary

When figuring out what the package actually exports, start at:

source/index.ts

rather than searching through every implementation file.

The package's generated entry point becomes:

distribution/index.js
distribution/index.d.ts

because package.json maps the package's exports to those files.

This distinction is useful when contributing:

source/ is the implementation; distribution/ is generated output.

You generally want to modify source/, not generated distribution files.

10. Understanding URL handling

Two options are easy to confuse:

baseUrl

baseUrl participates in normal URL resolution.

For example:

ky('users', {
	baseUrl: '/api/'
});

resolves users under /api/.

An absolute input URL bypasses baseUrl.

prefix

prefix is applied before URL resolution.

It is especially useful when you want /users to be treated as part of a prefixed API path rather than as an origin-relative URL.

The repository has separate tests for both:

test/base-url.ts
test/prefix.ts

So changes to URL resolution should generally be accompanied by tests in those areas.

11. Understanding retries

Retries are one of the more sophisticated parts of the project.

The flow is roughly:

request fails
    │
    ▼
Has retry budget remaining?
    │
    ├── no → throw
    │
    ▼
Is this a retriable error?
    │
    ├── no → throw
    │
    ▼
Calculate delay
    │
    ├── normal exponential backoff
    ├── jitter
    └── Retry-After / rate-limit timing
    │
    ▼
beforeRetry hooks
    │
    ├── stop → stop
    ├── Request → retry that request
    ├── Response → use that response
    └── otherwise → retry original operation

Ky.ts implements this in #calculateRetryDelay() and #retryFromError().

There is also an explicit ky.retry() mechanism. An afterResponse hook can return it to force another attempt, including with a custom delay, error code, cause, or replacement Request.

Contributor tip: retry changes deserve extra caution. They interact with request bodies, streams, timeouts, hooks, response consumption, and resource cleanup.

12. Understanding hooks

Hooks are lifecycle extension points.

The core implementation has, among others:

init
beforeRequest
afterResponse
beforeRetry
beforeError

The request pipeline runs beforeRequest before Fetch.

After receiving a response, afterResponse hooks can:

inspect the response;
return a replacement response;
modify behavior;
request a retry with ky.retry().

The README also demonstrates using afterResponse for scenarios such as refreshing an authentication token after a 401 or retrying based on an error contained in a successful response body.

If you're modifying hooks, read both:

source/core/Ky.ts
source/utils/merge.ts
test/hooks.ts

because hook behavior involves both execution and inheritance/merging.

13. How the tests are organized

The tests are mostly feature-oriented rather than mirroring the source directory.

Examples:

Test	What it covers
main.ts	General/core API behavior
methods.ts	HTTP method shortcuts
fetch.ts	Fetch integration/custom fetch
headers.ts	Headers
base-url.ts	baseUrl resolution
prefix.ts	prefix behavior
retry.ts	Retry behavior
hooks.ts	Lifecycle hooks
http-error.ts	HTTP errors
body-size.ts	Response/error body limits
stream.ts	Streaming
browser.ts	Browser-specific behavior
bytes.ts	Response.bytes() behavior
formdata-searchparams.ts	FormData/search parameter handling
memory-leak.ts	Resource/memory cleanup
context.ts	Request context
with-page.ts	Browser/page helpers

The repository's test structure lists these files explicitly.

14. Test infrastructure

The test suite uses AVA.

package.json configures TypeScript files as ES modules and tells AVA to load tsx/esm:

AVA
 └── tsx/esm
      └── TypeScript tests

Worker threads are disabled.

Local HTTP server

Many tests don't call arbitrary external APIs. Instead, the test helpers create an Express HTTP server dynamically.

create-http-test-server.ts:

creates an Express application;
creates an HTTP server;
listens on a dynamically assigned port;
exposes server.url;
automatically closes the server through AVA teardown when given a test context.

This is a useful pattern to follow when adding HTTP behavior tests: create a deterministic local endpoint rather than depending on an external service.

Browser tests

test/helpers/with-page.ts integrates Playwright and supports:

Chromium
Firefox
WebKit

The helper defines browser-specific test and cleanup timeouts.

This explains why CI explicitly installs Playwright browsers before npm test.

15. Running individual tests

Because the project uses AVA, you can invoke AVA directly.

For example:

npx ava test/retry.ts

or:

npx ava test/hooks.ts

For debugging browser-related tests, the repository provides:

npm run debug

which sets PWDEBUG=1 and runs AVA with a two-minute timeout.

You can also run AVA directly with its filtering options when investigating a particular test.

16. Linting and type/build validation

The repository uses XO for linting:

npx xo

npm test runs XO before building and testing, so contributors normally don't need to invoke it separately.

TypeScript is configured through the Sindre Sorhus shared TypeScript configuration:

"extends": "@sindresorhus/tsconfig"

with exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled.

The distribution build changes only the output configuration:

rootDir: source
outDir: distribution
sourceMap: true
inlineSources: true

17. A good first contribution workflow

For a new contributor, I'd recommend this sequence:

Step 1 — Install

npm install
npx playwright install --with-deps

Step 2 — Verify the baseline

npm test

If this fails before you've changed anything, investigate the environment first.

Step 3 — Read the public API

Start with:

readme.md
source/index.ts
source/types/options.ts
source/types/hooks.ts
source/types/retry.ts

The README is particularly useful because it documents the intended behavior and contains examples. The repository explicitly describes Ky as a Fetch-based client and notes its support for browsers, Node.js, Bun, and Deno.

Step 4 — Read the core pipeline

Then read:

source/core/Ky.ts
source/core/constants.ts
source/core/retry-timing.ts

Don't start by reading every utility. Ky.ts gives you the architectural map.

Step 5 — Find the corresponding tests

If you're changing:

retry      → test/retry.ts
hooks      → test/hooks.ts
URL logic  → test/base-url.ts / test/prefix.ts
methods    → test/methods.ts
errors     → test/http-error.ts
streams    → test/stream.ts
browser    → test/browser.ts

This is usually the fastest way to understand the intended behavior.

Step 6 — Make the smallest change

Keep the change focused. Ky's core has a lot of carefully handled interactions around retries, streams, abort signals, timeouts, and response bodies.

Step 7 — Add/regress a test

For a bug fix, first identify the behavior that should fail without your change. Add a regression test that expresses that behavior.

Step 8 — Run the narrow test

For example:

npx ava test/retry.ts

Then run:

npm test

before considering the change complete.

18. Things to be especially careful about

Request bodies and retries

The implementation deliberately clones requests in preparation for retries, but avoids unnecessary cloning when retries are disabled because cloning streams can buffer data in memory.

So seemingly harmless retry changes can have memory/performance consequences.

Timeouts

There are two concepts:

timeout
    per attempt
totalTimeout
    entire operation, including retries and delays

Don't accidentally implement one in terms of the other.

Response-body consumption

Ky decorates the returned response and implements timeout handling around body reads. It also has explicit cleanup logic for streams and cloned responses.

This is one reason memory-leak.ts and stream.ts are valuable tests rather than incidental extras.

HTTP errors versus Fetch failures

A server returning 500 is fundamentally different from Fetch failing because the network connection failed. The repository has separate error classes and retry paths for those cases.

Browser capability differences

Don't assume a Node implementation is sufficient. Ky explicitly feature-detects streams, abort APIs, FormData, and other Fetch functionality.

19. CI expectations

The GitHub Actions workflow is a useful description of what maintainers consider the canonical validation environment:

Node 22
Node 24
latest Node
      │
      ▼
npm install
      │
      ▼
Playwright browsers
      │
      ▼
npm test

The workflow runs on push and pull_request and uses macOS runners.

So if your local change passes:

npm test

with Node 22+, you've reproduced the core CI command, although not necessarily every CI matrix environment.

20. Mental model for the codebase

If you only remember one map of the repository, use this:

                     ┌──────────────────┐
                     │  source/index.ts │
                     │   Public API     │
                     └────────┬─────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                     ┌──────────────────┐
                     │   core/Ky.ts     │
                     │ Request pipeline │
                     └───────┬──────────┘
                             │
          ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
          ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     types/*             utils/*           errors/*
   Public contracts    Implementation       Error model
          │                  │                  │
          └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                             ▼
                        Fetch / Request
                             │
                             ▼
                         Response
                             │
                             ▼
                       retry + hooks
                             │
                             ▼
                     decorated response
     test/
       │
       ├── feature tests ───────────► source behavior
       ├── local HTTP server ───────► deterministic requests
       └── Playwright helpers ──────► browser behavior

In short: start with readme.md and source/index.ts, learn the request lifecycle in source/core/Ky.ts, then use the feature-specific tests as executable documentation. The build produces distribution/; contributors should normally work in source/. The one-command validation path is npm test, which runs linting, the TypeScript build, and AVA.
